Let \(g(x)=f'(x)\). Since \(f\) is increasing and invertible, the inverse function theorem gives

\[
(f^{-1})'(f(x))=\frac{1}{f'(x)}=\frac{1}{g(x)}.
\]

The differential inequality becomes

\[
g'(x)+2g(x)\ge 2,\qquad g(0)=2.
\]

Multiply by the integrating factor \(e^{2x}\):

\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x}g(x)\right)\ge 2e^{2x}.
\]

Integrate from \(0\) to \(x\):

\[
e^{2x}g(x)-2 \ge \int_0^x 2e^{2t}\,dt=e^{2x}-1.
\]

Thus

\[
e^{2x}g(x)\ge e^{2x}+1
\]

and therefore

\[
g(x)\ge 1+e^{-2x}.
\]

Hence

\[
(f^{-1})'(f(x))=\frac{1}{g(x)}
\le \frac{1}{1+e^{-2x}}<1
\]

for every finite \(x\). So \(1\) is an upper bound.

This bound is sharp. For example, take

\[
f(x)=x+\frac12(1-e^{-2x}).
\]

Then

\[
f'(x)=1+e^{-2x},\qquad f''(x)=-2e^{-2x},
\]

so

\[
f''(x)+2f'(x)=2,\qquad f'(0)=2,
\]

and \(f\) is strictly increasing and invertible. For this function,

\[
(f^{-1})'(f(x))=\frac{1}{1+e^{-2x}}\to 1
\quad\text{as }x\to\infty.
\]

Thus the least upper bound is \(1\). Strictly speaking, it is not attained at any finite \(x\), so it is a supremum; the intended maximum value is

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
